units.title: Hello, Odin!
units.summary: Write your first Odin program and print text and numbers with fmt.println and fmt.printf.

lesson.md: Odin is a simple and fast programming language. This course uses Odin `dev-2026-11`, the release from November 2026. Every Odin program is made of **packages**. A program that you can run uses `package main` and has a procedure called `main`. Odin starts the program there.

Line by line: `package main` says that this file belongs to the main package. `import "core:fmt"` loads the `fmt` package, which can print text. The prefix `core:` means that the package comes with Odin. `main :: proc()` defines the procedure `main`: `::` means "is defined as" and `proc` means procedure. Its code goes between the braces `{` and `}`.

`fmt.println` prints its values, puts a space between them and ends the line. Text goes in double quotes and is called a **string**. Numbers have no quotes. `fmt.println()` without values prints an empty line.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    fmt.println("Odin", "is", "fun")
    fmt.println(1, 2, 3)
    fmt.println()
    fmt.println("Done")
}

lesson.md: Odin can calculate for you. `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is only text. Use `*` to multiply and `/` to divide.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    fmt.println(2 + 3)
    fmt.println("2 + 3")
    fmt.println(7 * 6)
}

lesson.md: `fmt.printf` prints a **format string** and fills in values. Each placeholder starts with `%`: `%s` for a string, `%d` for a whole number and `%v` for any value. `printf` does not end the line, so you add `\n` (a new line) yourself. `fmt.printfln` works the same way but ends the line for you.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    fmt.printf("%s is %d years old.\n", "Ada", 36)
    fmt.printfln("%v, %v and %v", "text", 42, true)
    fmt.printf("One line. ")
    fmt.printf("Same line.\n")
}
lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
text, 42 and true
One line. Same line.

lesson.md: A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and Odin ignores it. You do not need a semicolon `;` at the end of a line.
Odin is case sensitive: `fmt.println` works, `fmt.Println` does not exist. Text needs double quotes: `"Hi"` is a string, `'Hi'` is an error.

card: `package main` + `main :: proc()` make a runnable program
`fmt.println(a, b)` prints with spaces and a new line
`fmt.printf("%s %d %v\n", s, n, x)` fills in values

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, get to know int, f64, string and bool, and fix values with constants.

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name. `name := value` creates a new variable: `:=` declares it and gives it its first value. Later, `=` changes the value of a variable that already exists.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    name := "Ada"
    age := 36
    fmt.println(name, "is", age)
    age = 37
    fmt.println(age)
}

lesson.md: Every variable has a **type**, and it never changes. `int` holds whole numbers, `f64` decimal numbers, `string` text and `bool` the values `true` or `false`. With `:=` Odin picks the type from the value. You can also write it yourself: `name: type = value`. A variable without a value starts with its **zero value**: `0` for numbers and `false` for `bool`.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    count: int = 3
    price: f64 = 2.5
    title: string = "Odin"
    done: bool = true
    empty: int
    fmt.println(count, price, title, done, empty)
}

lesson.md: Odin knows `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and `%` gives the remainder of a division. When you divide two `int` values, Odin drops the remainder: `7 / 2` is `3`. With decimal numbers, `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`. `x += 5` is short for `x = x + 5`; `-=`, `*=` and `/=` work the same way.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    fmt.println(7 / 2, 7 % 2)
    fmt.println(7.0 / 2)
    x := 10
    x += 5
    fmt.println(x)
}

lesson.md: Odin never mixes types on its own: an `int` plus an `f64` is an error. You convert a value with the name of the type, like a procedure call: `f64(n)` makes a decimal number, `int(x)` makes a whole number and drops the decimals.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    n := 7
    half := f64(n) / 2
    price := 9.99
    fmt.println(half, int(price))
}

lesson.md: `::` declares a **constant**: a value that is fixed when the program is compiled. You cannot change a constant later. You already know `::` from `main :: proc()`: the procedure `main` is a constant too.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    MAX :: 100
    GREETING :: "Hi"
    fmt.println(GREETING, MAX * 2)
}

lesson.md: `:=` creates a new variable, `=` changes an existing one. Using `:=` twice for the same name in the same block is an error. Odin has no `x++`: write `x += 1`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program decide with if, else and switch, and combine conditions with &&, || and !.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition needs no parentheses, but the code always goes between braces `{` and `}`.
A comparison gives a `bool`. `==` means equal, `!=` not equal, and there are `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Note the difference: `=` changes a variable, `==` compares two values.
`else` runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if` you test more conditions one after the other. Odin runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.
You can combine conditions: `&&` means and (both must be `true`), `||` means or (at least one must be `true`), and `!` turns `true` into `false` and the other way round.

`switch` compares one value with several cases. A `case` can list several values, separated by commas. `case:` without a value is the default: it runs when no other case matches. Odin runs only the matching case and never continues into the next one, so you need no `break`.
A `switch` without a value works like a chain of `if` and `else if`: every case is a condition, and the first `true` one runs.
The condition must be a `bool`. `if 1 { }` is an error, and so is `if x = 5 { }`: write `if x == 5 { }`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with the for loop: counting, ranges, loops with a condition, break and continue.

lesson.md: Odin has only one loop keyword: `for`. The classic form has three parts, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step.
`i := 0` runs once at the start. Odin checks `i < 3` before every round and stops when it is `false`. `i += 1` runs after every round. Each run of the loop body is called an **iteration**.
A **range** is shorter: `for i in 0..<3` counts `0`, `1`, `2`. The `..<` stops before the end. With `..=` the end is included, so `1..=3` counts `1`, `2`, `3`.
A `for` with only a condition repeats as long as the condition is `true`. Other languages call this a while loop.
A `for` without anything repeats forever. `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one.
A common pattern: a variable outside the loop collects a result, and every iteration adds to it.
Odin has no `i++`, so the classic loop needs `i += 1`. The three parts have no parentheses around them.

units.title: Procedures
units.summary: Write your own procedures with parameters and return values, including procedures that return several values.

lesson.md: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run (call) as often as you like. You declare it like `main`: a name, `::` and `proc`. To call it, write its name and parentheses.

**Parameters** are the inputs of a procedure. Each one has a name and a type, like `name: string`. Several parameters with the same type can share it: `a, b: int`. The values you pass when you call the procedure are called **arguments**.

`-> int` after the parameters says that the procedure gives back an `int`. `return` ends the procedure and gives the value back to the caller. You can store the result in a variable or use it directly.

A procedure can return several values. Put the types in parentheses, `-> (int, int)`, and separate the values with commas after `return`. The caller receives them with several names: `q, r := divide(17, 5)`.
Odin code often returns a `bool` as the last value to say if everything worked. The caller can then check `ok`.
The order of procedures in the file does not matter. `main` can call a procedure that is declared below it.
Parameters cannot be changed inside the procedure: `n = 5` is an error when `n` is a parameter. If you need a changeable copy, write `n := n` at the start of the procedure.

units.title: Arrays and slices
units.summary: Store many values in fixed arrays, look at parts of them with slices, and grow lists with dynamic arrays.

lesson.md: A **fixed array** holds a fixed number of values of one type. `[3]int` is an array of three `int` values. You reach an element with its **index** in square brackets. The first index is `0`. `len(a)` gives the number of elements.
`for value in arr` goes through all elements. With `for value, i in arr` you also get the index. Note the order: the value comes first, then the index.

A **slice** is a view of a part of an array. Its type is written without a size, like `[]int`. `a[1:4]` starts at index `1` and stops before index `4`. `a[:2]` starts at the beginning, `a[3:]` goes to the end. A slice does not copy the values: when you change the slice, you change the array.

A **dynamic array**, like `[dynamic]int`, can grow. `append(&list, value)` adds values at the end. The `&` gives `append` the address of the variable, so it can change it. A dynamic array uses memory that you give back with `delete(list)`. `defer` runs a line at the end of the procedure, so you can write `defer delete(list)` right after you create the list.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    list: [dynamic]int
    defer delete(list)
    append(&list, 5)
    append(&list, 7, 9)
    fmt.println(list, len(list))
}

lesson.md: A procedure that takes a slice works with every kind of array. Write `arr[:]` to pass a whole array or dynamic array as a slice.
An index must be smaller than the length. In `[3]int` the last index is `2`, and `a[3]` is an error. A fixed array cannot grow: only dynamic arrays work with `append`.

units.title: Structs and enums
units.summary: Group values in structs, change them through pointers, and use enums with switch.

lesson.md: A **struct** groups several values under one name. You declare it with `::` and `struct`. Each **field** has a name and a type, and a comma follows each field. You reach a field with a dot: `p.x`.
You can name the fields when you create a struct: `Player{name = "Ada", level = 2}`. Fields that you leave out get their zero value.

A procedure gets a copy of a struct. To change the original, pass a **pointer**: the type `^Player` means "pointer to a `Player`", and `&hero` gives the address of `hero`. Through the pointer, `p.level` reaches the field of the original.
An **enum** is a type with a fixed list of named values. You write a value as `Direction.East`. When Odin already knows the type, `.West` is enough. `println` prints the name of the value.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

Direction :: enum {
    North,
    East,
    South,
    West,
}

main :: proc() {
    d := Direction.East
    fmt.println(d)
    d = .West
    fmt.println(d, d == .West)
}

lesson.md: A `switch` over an enum has one case for each value. Odin checks that you did not forget a value: a missing case is an error.
If you really want to handle only some values, write `#partial switch` instead of `switch`.
Assigning a struct copies it: after `q := p`, changing `q.x` does not change `p.x`. Use a pointer when you want to change the original.

units.title: Maps and strings
units.summary: Look up values by key with maps, and work with text using len, slices and the strings package.

lesson.md: A **map** stores values under **keys**. `map[string]int` has `string` keys and `int` values. You create a map with `make`, and you give its memory back with `delete`. `m[key] = value` adds or changes an entry, and `m[key]` reads it.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    ages := make(map[string]int)
    defer delete(ages)
    ages["Ada"] = 36
    ages["Linus"] = 28
    fmt.println(ages["Ada"], len(ages))
}

lesson.md: A key that is not in the map gives the zero value. To find out if a key exists, write `value, ok := m[key]`: `ok` is `true` only when the key exists. `key in m` gives the same answer. `delete_key(&m, key)` removes an entry.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"

main :: proc() {
    stock := make(map[string]int)
    defer delete(stock)
    stock["apple"] = 5
    n, ok := stock["pear"]
    fmt.println(n, ok)
    fmt.println("apple" in stock)
    delete_key(&stock, "apple")
    fmt.println(len(stock))
}

lesson.md: `for key, value in m` goes through all entries. The order of the entries is not fixed, so do not rely on it. The name `_` throws away a value that you do not need.

For a `string`, `len(s)` gives its length in bytes. For English letters, that is the number of characters. `s[1:3]` is a part of the string, like a slice of an array. `for c in s` goes through the characters one by one.

The package `core:strings` has helpers for text. `strings.contains` and `strings.has_prefix` answer with a `bool`, and `strings.index` gives the position of a text, or `-1` if it is not there. `strings.to_upper` creates a new string, so give its memory back with `delete`.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"
import "core:strings"

main :: proc() {
    text := "Hello, Odin"
    fmt.println(strings.contains(text, "Odin"))
    fmt.println(strings.index(text, "o"))
    fmt.println(strings.has_prefix(text, "Hell"))
    upper := strings.to_upper(text)
    defer delete(upper)
    fmt.println(upper)
}

lesson.md: `strings.split` cuts a string into a slice of strings. `strings.join` puts strings together with a separator between them. Both create new memory.

lesson.code:
package main

import "core:fmt"
import "core:strings"

main :: proc() {
    parts := strings.split("red,green,blue", ",")
    defer delete(parts)
    fmt.println(len(parts), parts[1])
    joined := strings.join(parts, " + ")
    defer delete(joined)
    fmt.println(joined)
}

lesson.md: `+` joins only fixed texts like `"ab" + "cd"`. For variables, use `strings.concatenate({a, b})`.
